```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Airbnb
```{r}
data("nyc_airbnb")

nyc_airbnb = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate( 
    stars = review_scores_location / 2
  ) |> 
  rename(
    borough = neighbourhood_group,
    neighborhood = neighbourhood
  ) |> 
  filter(
    borough != "Staten Island"
  ) |> 
  select(
    price, stars, borough, neighborhood, room_type
  )

nyc_airbnb
```
eliminating Staten island because we just don't want to base model on an item that has very few data points

## Fit a model
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = price, color = borough)) +
  geom_point()
```

Let's fit the model that we care about

#linear regression
```{r}
fit = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
```

What we have done? Let's look at result...
```{r}
fit
summary(fit)
summary(fit)$coef
coef(fit)

#fitted.values(fit)
#resid(fit)
names(summary(fit))
```

Names of things in fit
  -some stuff that goes along: what is rank, what is df residual, etc
Linear model saves a bunch of stuff in the background - helpful to know its their

most of the output is bad, but sometimes it's useful

Let's look at the results better...

```{r}
broom::glance(fit)

broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  mutate(
    term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
bronx is automatically the reference group
-broom function super useful, broom pulls out this useful information
  -broom::glance(fit) - gives you very quick look at information that is helpful. 
  
## Be in control of factors:
  -borough variable is a character variable: usually converted into factor variable
    -factor variable: string label lying on top of number affixed to it. If not careful: R will do best guess
    
Change reference category for interested variables
  -reference group is one with most airbnb rentals
  -room type = factor variable, wichever one is most common
  
```{r}
nyc_airbnb_infreq=
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    borough = fct_infreq(borough),
    room_type = fct_infreq(room_type)
  )
nyc_airbnb_infreq |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = price, color = borough)) +
  geom_point()
```
  -Manhattan > Brooklyn > Queens > Bronx most 
  
Refit model
```{r}
fit_infreq= lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb_infreq)
fit_infreq

broom::tidy(fit_infreq) |> 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough:")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

  broom::glance(fit_infreq)
```
-previously comparing everything to the Bronx, now comparing everything to Manhattan
  -hasn't substantially changed what is happening

## Diagnostics
  -up until this point doing residuals of fit
    -want variables and tack on residuals and fitted values
diagnostics is basically "look at the residuals"
  
```{r}
modelr::add_residuals(nyc_airbnb_infreq, fit)
```
Adding in a column called resid: worry about residuals and residual distribution
  now have residuals based on model fit: distribution of residuals


We can look at residuals
```{r}
nyc_airbnb_infreq |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit_infreq) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = resid)) +
  geom_violin() +
  ylim(-500, 1500)

nyc_airbnb_infreq |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit_infreq) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(. ~ borough)
```
model will have outliers. But the residuals seem to be incredibly large
  -issues that come in because we have huge outliers
  > some issue in model try to find error

Residuals are skewed:
  -much more spread in 5 stars vs 3 stars

With regression with large samples everything becomes equally distributed
  -shouldn't trust CI that come out of this

## Hypothesis testing

```{r}
fit_infreq |> 
broom::tidy() |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
R doing hypothesis test on estimate with standard error, statistics, p value
  -can also do a p test
Categorical predictor with mult levels: not ask if individual levels differ from the reference group
  -if predictor or categorical value as a whole is significnt in the context of my model

broom::tidy() does t test by default

What about the significance of "borough"
  F test or ANOVA
    -fit_null = lm(price ~ stars)
      -if null hypothesis borough is not associated with price
      -alternative model: lm(price ~ stars + borugh, data = nyc_airbnb) 

Permutation testing - when you don't trust the assumptions you should use this
Is brough significant: can't look at individual values need to look at whole thing

Try testing nested model

```{r}
fit_infreq_null = lm(price ~ stars, data = nyc_airbnb)
fit_infreq_alt = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
  
anova(fit_infreq_null, fit_infreq_alt) |> 
  broom::tidy()
```

## Nesting data, fit models
Fit interactions: slope on stars and boroughs
  -interactions important, complicated to understand

different from nesting models - 
```{r}
fit_nest =
  nyc_airbnb_infreq |> 
  lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

fit_nest
```
looking at relation
does stars differ if its in Brooklyn vs Manhattan
  -how does reference of room type differ from reference category:
    -shared room type for Manhattan seems to have a much cheaper type
  -difference between private room and entire apartment in Brooklyn
    -take overall effect and add to the interested data point
Framework of interactions: assess stat sig, compare stat with interactions to not to see if it fits
  -test important and unimportant

Pretty formal and complicated
```{r}
fit = lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type * borough, data = nyc_airbnb_infreq) |> 
  broom::tidy()

fit
```

This is more exploratory but maybe easier to understand:
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(data = -borough)
```
Tibble with boroughs with entire data frame in other column
  -can you fit a model to this (Manhattan, Queens, etc) list column
    -with map and mutate

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(data = -borough) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(.x = data, ~lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = .x)),
    results = map(models, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(-data, -models) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term != "Intercept") |> 
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = borough,
    values_from = estimate
  )
```
going from entire apartment to private room will save you 53 in Bronx
    
What if I want to know what's happening in Manhattan?
```{r}
nyc_airbnb_infreq |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()

nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Bronx") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()
```

Nest even more:
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  nest(data = -neighborhood) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(.x = data, ~lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = .x)),
    results = map(models, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(-data, -models) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(str_detect(term, "room_type")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = neighborhood, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(. ~ term) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 70, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```
